issues.title: core: bound ws/wss/socks handshakes with a dial timeout
issues.body:
## Summary

Only the plain TCP dial is bounded (5 s). After the TCP connection succeeds:

- the WebSocket HTTP upgrade has **no deadline**;
- the WSS TLS handshake has **no deadline** (the default `TLSHandshakeTimeout` of 10 s does not apply because the transport is built by hand);
- the SOCKS negotiation has **no deadline**.

A peer — or a middlebox — that accepts the TCP connection but never completes the handshake therefore holds the dial open until the peer is removed entirely, wasting the whole backoff cycle on a dead attempt.

## Fix

Introduce a shared `wsDialTimeout` (15 s, a variable so tests can shorten it) and apply it to each stage:

- `http.Client.Timeout` for the ws/wss upgrade (the websocket library turns it into a deadline for the handshake only, so the upgraded connection is not affected);
- `TLSHandshakeTimeout` for the WSS TLS handshake, which also bounds a dial the transport may finish in the background after the request is cancelled;
- a context-bounded SOCKS negotiation via `DialContext` when the proxy supports it (the `x/net` SOCKS5 dialer does).

Files: `src/core/link_ws.go`, `src/core/link_wss.go`, `src/core/link_socks.go`.

## Tests

- `TestWSDialTimeout`, `TestWSSDialTimeout`, `TestSOCKSDialTimeout`: a server accepts TCP and never answers; each dial must be abandoned at the timeout (1 s in the tests). Without the change all three fail.
- `TestWSDialTimeoutSparesUpgradedConn`: an upgraded ws/wss connection keeps working after the timeout has passed.
- The shared test logger now sets its call depth up front: `gologme/log` sets it lazily on first output, which the race detector flags when several goroutines log for the first time at once.

`go test ./...` passes, and the new tests pass under `-race`.

Closing the per-dial transport, so that cancelled dials do not leave sockets behind, is a separate follow-up: #1383.

issues.title: core: close the per-dial transport of ws/wss dials
issues.body:
## Summary

When a ws/wss dial is cancelled or times out, `net/http` may keep finishing the dial in the background and park the connection in the transport's idle pool. Each dial creates its own `http.Transport` and drops it afterwards, so these sockets stay open after the dial has returned: a cancelled WS dial left its socket open for more than 10 s in testing, and a WSS dial keeps it until the TLS handshake timeout.

## Fix

Defer `CloseIdleConnections()` on the per-dial transport in `src/core/link_ws.go` and `src/core/link_wss.go`. It closes idle connections and cancels dials still in progress. The upgraded connection is not in the pool and is not affected (`TestWSDialTimeoutSparesUpgradedConn` from #1381 keeps passing).

## Test

`TestDialCancelClosesSocket` cancels ws, wss and socks dials stuck in the handshake and requires each to return and close its socket within a second:

- without the change: ws and wss fail (socket left open), socks passes;
- with the change: all pass.

`go test ./...` passes; the dial tests also pass under `-race`.

This builds on #1381 and includes its commit until that is merged; only the last commit is new.

Fixes #7131

## What

- Bump `refraction-networking/utls` from `aa6edf4` to `6ebdceb` (2026-10-06, no tagged release yet — same pinned-commit pattern as the current `aa6edf4` pin) and add `"hellochrome_155"` to `ModernFingerprints`.

A small program calling it in the same Termux prints `route ip+net: netlinkrib: permission denied`. go-nat drops discovery errors, so the realm log only shows `no NAT found`, and it shows it before any SSDP wait could happen. Every go-nat path runs into it: goupnp's `DiscoverDevicesCtx` picks SSDP source addresses with `net.Interfaces()` (`localIPv4MCastAddrs`), koron/go-ssdp's `Search` lists interfaces with it too, and go-netroute (NAT-PMP) dumps routes over netlink. `DiscoverGateway` ends with `ErrNoNATFound`. issues.title: [Proposal] Plugin System based on WASM (wazero) for Hot-Patching Protocols & Logic on Mobile
issues.body:
Mobile clients (especially iOS) suffer from long App Store review cycles. When a critical bug is found in the core, or when GFW introduces new active probing that requires immediate protocol adjustments, users are left without connection for weeks until a new binary is reviewed and released.

Currently, Xray is monolithic. We cannot update internal logic without replacing the binary. On iOS, dynamic linking of native binaries is strictly forbidden by the OS sandbox.

I propose integrating a pure Go WebAssembly runtime, such as [wazero](https://github.com/wazero/wazero), into Xray-core.

The goal is to define a set of interfaces (hooks) for:
1. Protocol Handlers / Transports (Dialers & Listeners)
2. Obfuscation Logic (Packet manipulation)
3. Routing Rules

Xray should be able to load external `.wasm` modules at runtime (fetched from a remote URL or local storage).

**How it solves the problem:**
1. **Compliance:** WASM is interpreted code, which is allowed by Apple's App Store guidelines (unlike native dlopen).
2. **Hot-Fixes:** Developers can compile a fix (written in Go/Rust/TinyGo) to WASM and push it to clients immediately via a config update.
3. **Flexibility:** We can patch specific logic flaws (for example, the recent problem #5230) without waiting for a full app release.

**Alternatives considered**
- **Starlark/Lua scripting:** Good for routing, but too slow for heavy packet processing/crypto hooks.
- **Go Plugins:** Not supported on mobile architectures and incompatible with iOS security policies.

This architecture would make Xray significantly more resilient against censorship events, allowing the community to deploy countermeasures instantly to millions of mobile users.

issues.title: XHTTP stream-up behind an HTTP/1.1 Nginx upstream truncates uploads
issues.body:
### Integrity requirements

- [x] I have read all the comments in the issue template and ensured that this issue meet the requirements.
- [x] I confirm that I have read the documentation, understand the meaning of all the configuration items I wrote, and did not pile up seemingly useful options or default values.
- [x] I provided the complete config and logs, rather than just providing the truncated parts based on my own judgment.
- [x] I searched issues and did not find any similar issues.
- [x] The problem can be successfully reproduced in the latest Release

### Description

Large uploads through XHTTP `stream-up` fail for me when Nginx forwards the XHTTP requests to Xray over HTTP/1.1. Curl reports that it sent the whole body, but the destination receives only part of it, or the connection fails before the destination can parse the request.

I reduced this to a local Docker setup with a synthetic JSON body. There is no CDN, external API, authentication header, or TLS in the minimal reproduction.

Tested versions:
- Xray main, commit `0f3d884786f9ec73d3be8899cb6b9e1e6dd3c41e`.
- Binary: `Xray 26.10.10 Custom (go1.27.1 linux/amd64)`.
- Nginx image: `nginx:1.28-alpine`.
- Curl image: `curlimages/curl:8.12.1`.
- I also reproduced the HTTP/1.1 problem on Xray v26.3.27 / Go 1.26.1.

The test body is 1,385,909 bytes. In the minimal run shown in the logs, the destination received **7,999 bytes followed by EOF**, while curl reported the full upload and got HTTP 503 after about 5 ms. The received length varies between runs. I expected the destination to receive the complete body and return HTTP 200.

Two changes make the same test pass:
- Set `scStreamUpServerSecs: -1` on the XHTTP **server inbound**. This disables the POST response keepalive, so it has an idle-timeout trade-off.
- Leave response keepalive enabled, but change Nginx's backend hop to HTTP/2 using `grpc_pass`. Xray still uses XHTTP `stream-up`, not the gRPC transport.

On the main build, the original HTTP/1.1 setup delivered 0/10 bodies intact. Disabling response keepalive passed 4/4. HTTP/2 upstream passed 6/6 fast uploads and another 2/2 uploads limited to 32 KiB/s, lasting about 42 seconds each. For those slow tests I set the server response padding interval to one second. The HTTP/2 tests covered HTTP forwarding and HTTPS CONNECT with synthetic bodies. The release v26.3.27 also passed 4/4 fast HTTP/2-upstream tests. Direct XHTTP without Nginx passed both control probes.

I suspect the early POST response interacts with Go's HTTP/1 request-body handling. The server log contains `http: invalid Read on closed Body`. The stream-up handler reads the POST body while writing response padding, without enabling HTTP/1 full duplex. Nginx removes the client's `Connection: close` header in this setup, so the backend is taking a different HTTP/1 response path from the direct connection.

This is not a confirmed complete explanation: I also tested an experimental `EnableFullDuplex` change, and it only passed 4/10 probes; the others stalled after receiving a body prefix. On the v26.3.27 baseline, a full capture showed that Nginx received and forwarded identical decoded POST bodies, yet bytes were missing at the destination. So I do not think the evidence points to Nginx simply dropping bytes from the upload.

Relevant handler: https://github.com/XTLS/Xray-core/blob/0f3d884786f9ec73d3be8899cb6b9e1e6dd3c41e/transport/internet/splithttp/hub.go#L198-L242

Could the concurrent POST body reads and response keepalive writes be handled differently for HTTP/1 upstreams?

issues.body:
builds on the lua engine from #6823 and the noise hook from #7124, docs will follow once #909 is merged

-- `header-custom` takes a `script`, which can't be set together with `clients`, `servers`, `errors` or the udp `client`, `server`. the script's path resolves like the other lua ones and `infra` only compiles it, so a typo is caught at startup while the pool is created the first time a layer needs a header
-- tcp: `HandleHeader(stream, address, role)` runs the whole handshake, `stream:Write(bytes)`, `stream:Read(size)` and `stream:Sleep(ms)`. `role` is `client` or `server`, so one file serves both ends like the static config does. returning an error fails the connection, which is what `header auth failed` already does, and a server can `stream:Write` a fake answer before it returns, the way the static `errors` sequences work
-- udp: `HandleHeaderWrite(header, address, role)` builds the prefix with `header:Add(bytes)` and `header:AddRandom(size)`, `HandleHeaderRead(packet, address, role)` returns how many bytes to strip, or nil to drop the packet, and reads it through `packet:Len()`, `packet:Byte(at)`, `packet:Match(at, bytes)` and `packet:Slice(from, to)`
-- no new module: the engine registers the public `RegisterLua` of `xray.finalmask.noise`, so a header script gets `Random` and `RandomBetween` from there, plus `xray.log`

no LTable on either path, one stream, one builder and one packet view per instance, reused, and the numbers are checked: a handshake takes at most 65535 bytes in and 65535 out, a udp header at most 1024, and every size, index and delay is validated before it is converted so a huge float or a nan can't slip through. a shared config can't make the hooks allocate without bound

`BenchmarkLuaHeader` is in the package: per packet a udp header costs about ten times the static one, 424 bytes in eight allocations against 24 in three, so the static lists stay the better choice at high packet rates. the tcp hook runs once per connection

timeouts: 30s for a handshake because it waits for the peer, 1s per udp packet, and the instance init stays 120s

issues.title: Finalmask: Add the `lua` mask (noise's `script` moves there)
issues.body:
#7174 bolted a second Lua mask onto header-custom, which was the wrong way around. One `lua` mask covers all of it now: it is both a `tcpMasks` and a `udpMasks` entry, and the script decides what it does by the hooks it defines.

-- `HandleHeader(stream, address, role)`, TCP: a free handshake before any traffic, with `stream:Write`, `stream:Read` and `stream:Sleep`. Return a string or an error and the connection is dropped
-- `HandleHeaderWrite(header, address, role)` and `HandleHeaderRead(packet, address, role)`, UDP: prefix every packet with a header, and strip it on the other side by returning its length, or `nil` to drop the packet
-- `HandleNoise(plan, address, role)` is the old noise hook, so `noise`'s `script` is gone (it has not been in a release yet)
-- `role` is `client` or `server`, so one file serves both ends
-- a hook the script does not define is not wrapped at all: a noise only script leaves TCP connections alone and never touches a packet
-- the module is `xray.finalmask` now, with `Random` and `RandomBetween`

```json
{
    "udpMasks": [{"type": "lua", "settings": {"script": "mask.lua", "reset": "30-60"}}]
}
```

Per call it takes at most 64 noise packets and 65535 bytes of noise, 1024 bytes of header, and 65535 bytes each way in a handshake. A packet hook gets 1s, a handshake 30s. A UDP header is one Lua call per packet, the benchmarks in the package cover its cost.

The static lists can follow later, the same script can already do what they do.

issues.title: Proposal: user-configurable traffic shaping profiles for XMC / FinalMask (follow-up to #6487)
issues.body:
The #6487 summary ends with:

> This intentionally does not emit version-specific Play or Chunk Data packets. **User-configurable traffic shaping is deferred to a follow-up PR.**

In the merge discussion @RPRX also noted that custom traffic-shape configuration would be added later as an incremental feature (流量形状自定义配置下次再补吧，毕竟是增量功能).

This issue proposes a concrete design for that follow-up and asks for design agreement before any implementation (a draft PR would follow if the direction is acceptable). If the original XMC author already has shaping work in flight, happy to stand down and review/help instead.

## Problem

The current XMC shaping is a built-in model of one fixed target (uncompressed Minecraft 26.1.2 login/join). Two practical limits:

- Built-in models decay when the camouflage target's traffic shape evolves; updating them requires core releases.
- Different deployments may need different camouflage targets, but today the XMC shape is a compiled-in preset and is not configurable (other masks, e.g. fragment #6334 or header-custom #5920, already take declarative config).

The knobs that exist today are scattered across features and do not compose with XMC's directional shaping: freedom fragment `maxSplit` (#4998), XHTTP upload pacing (`minUploadInterval`, #3592) and its padding mechanism (#3643), fragment `lengths`/`delays` (#6334), and the programmable `header-custom` templates (#5920).

## Proposal

Make the XMC shaping data-driven: a declarative profile loaded from config, interpreted by a small engine in `finalmask` — no policy logic in core.

Sketch:

```jsonc
{
  "schema": "xray.shape@1",
  "name": "xmc-default",
  "version": 1,
  "phases": {
    "login": {
      "c2s": { "lenDist": [ /* sampled length histogram */ ] },
      "s2c": { "lenDist": [ /* ... */ ] },
      "keepAlive": { "iatMs": 1000, "jitterMs": 100 }
    }
    // phase transitions follow the existing protocol state machine
  }
}
```

Runtime invariants (deliberately conservative):

- Padding only ever increases record length; shortening is fragmentation, which stays a separate mask.
- Zero added latency for real data: the profile only rate-limits sends (`iatMs` as "not faster than") and fills pauses with dummies. Delay-based scheduling is explicitly out of scope here.
- The turn schedule stays alternating-direction (client first), exactly like the merged XMC padding schedule; a profile only controls lengths and cadence, never the message flow.
- `shape` composes with the other configured masks rather than replacing them; the chain order stays whatever the `finalmask.tcp` array says (noise in particular remains a standalone pre-data layer).
- Fail-closed: schema/`version` mismatch between endpoints aborts the connection.
- Length values the server must reproduce are carried in-band, inside the encrypted channel.

## What this is not

- Not a new protocol and not a wire-format change.
- Not ML in core: profiles are produced offline elsewhere; core only interprets a table. A separate profile repository and geodata-style distribution can come later — out of scope here.
- Not delay/jitter scheduling (possible follow-up after measurements).

## Questions

1. Config placement: a profile embedded in `streamSettings` (per inbound/outbound), or a named registry referenced by id?
2. Are the invariants above (especially zero-delay + padding-only) the intended direction for the follow-up, or was something broader planned?
3. If the direction is agreed, would a draft PR with a single built-in preset (reproducing today's XMC 26.1.2 shape as a profile), tests, and the still missing XMC config docs be the right first step?

Prior art for profile-driven shaping engines: Maybenot (Karlstad University, arXiv:2304.09510) — a padding engine driven by parameterized state machines; the offline-profile / online-interpreter split here follows the same reasoning at the proxy layer.

Refs: #6487 #6210 #4998 #3592 #3643 #6334 #5920

issues.title: XDRIVE transport: Add the Google Drive and "template" backend
issues.body:
This stacks on #6745. Until that one is merged the diff here also contains its commit.

### What it adds

A `Storage` implementation for Google Drive, selected with `"service": "Google Drive"`, where `remoteFolder` is a Drive folder id and `secrets` holds ClientID, ClientSecret and RefreshToken.

### No SDK

Plain `net/http`, zero new entries in `go.mod`. It sits behind the same five method `Storage` interface as the local backend, so another provider is one more file and still no dependency.

### How it works

Paths are flattened into single names, so `streams/abc/c2s/000000000.seg` becomes `streams~abc~c2s~000000000.seg`, because Drive has no cheap path lookup and creating nested folders would cost a request per level.

A name to id cache is filled from every listing, so a download costs one request instead of two. The access token is cached and refreshed on expiry or on a 401.

Requests are retried on 429 and 5xx with a jittered backoff capped at 2 seconds. Jitter matters here: at concurrency 32 every request hits the rate limit at the same moment, and synchronised retries only make it worse. A request whose context is already cancelled is not retried at all.

### Measurements

Both ends on a server in the Netherlands, against a real Google Drive account.

Raw storage:

* 4 sequential puts of 256 KiB: 199 KiB/s
* 8 parallel puts of 256 KiB: 1637 KiB/s
* 8 parallel gets of 256 KiB: 2453 KiB/s
* listing a folder of 13 objects: 250 ms
* an uploaded object becomes listable after about 200 ms, so the listing is fresh enough to drive the log

Transport, 10 MB pushed through the WAL:

* segment 128 KiB, concurrency 16: 1187 KiB/s
* segment 256 KiB, concurrency 16: 1513 KiB/s
* segment 256 KiB, concurrency 32: 1849 KiB/s
* segment 512 KiB, concurrency 32: 2111 KiB/s

Real proxy, curl through SOCKS into VLESS over XDRIVE over Google Drive:

* 50 MB in 21.6 s, 2258 KiB/s, about 18.5 Mbit/s, byte identical
* the first byte takes about 2 s, so bulk transfer is comfortable and interactive use is not

Mux, 30 parallel requests, which is roughly one web page:

* without mux: 23675 ms and 30 sessions
* with mux.cool at concurrency 8: 8605 ms and 4 sessions

Stability: 12 of 12 live runs against Drive.

### Tests

A fake Drive server on `httptest` covers upload, listing, download, delete, token caching and retries, and the whole transport is run over it. Live tests against a real account live in the same file and skip unless `XRAY_XDRIVE_DRIVE_SECRETS` points at a credentials file, so nothing here needs secrets in CI.

### Known limits

Credentials sit on the client, so this is for self hosted use. One outbound should enable mux.cool, otherwise every TCP connection becomes its own session with its own files. The HTTP client does not go through Xray's own dialer yet, so `sockopt` and a dialer proxy are not applied to Drive requests.

issues.title: Hysteria client: Reset stalled writes when the connection is closed
issues.body:
Fixes #7169.

A stream write blocked on the QUIC flow control window (the peer stopped reading) could never be released on teardown: `interConn.Close()` only cancelled the read side and called `Stream.Close()`. The FIN queued by `Close()` cannot be delivered while data is stuck behind the window, so the peer kept the stream's unread data occupying its share of the connection-level window until the whole QUIC connection died - with 3-4 stalled streams every TCP request over the client hung for minutes while UDP kept working.

Change: `interConn.Close()` now cancels the stream's write side (`CancelWrite`, i.e. RESET_STREAM) when a write is still in flight, so the blocked `Write` returns and the peer drops the stream's unread data and releases its share of the connection window (quic-go credits the connection-level window on reset). Cleanly finished sessions keep the plain close. A `closed` flag orders concurrent `Write`/`Close` and makes a repeated `Close()` a no-op.

Verification:
- Unit test `TestTCPStalledWriteClose` (added): stalled stream + `Close()` => the blocked write returns, a new stream on the same connection can send again (connection window released), and a cleanly finished stream still delivers all data + FIN. RED on main (`stalled write did not return after close`), GREEN with the change.
- End to end on loopback against a real hysteria v2.11.0 server, the scenario from the report (4 uploads to a target that stops reading after ~2 MB, aborted with `SO_LINGER 0`):
  - before (10879a4a): 11 fresh requests over ~43 s after the abort never succeed;
  - after: the first retry that lands after the aborted sessions' own idle timeout succeeds (~6 s after the abort with `connIdle` forced to 5 s in the test client).
- `go test ./transport/internet/hysteria/` passes; gofmt clean.

Scope: the aborted session is released when it ends (its own idle timeout, or any other teardown of the session) - the local abort itself is not observable once the writer is wedged, so the idle timeout is still the upper bound with stock servers; a server that closes stalled targets (HyNetworks/hysteria#1703) recovers faster.

Outbound: Close the handler when removing it; VLESS Reverse Proxy: Don't start after closing
issues.body:
`outbound.Manager.RemoveHandler`, which `xray api rmo` (`HandlerService.RemoveOutbound`) calls, deletes the handler from the map but never closes it, while `inbound.Manager.RemoveHandler` does. So whatever the removed outbound's `Close()` would release keeps running:

- WireGuard creates its TUN in the constructor (a kernel TUN when available, otherwise a gVisor stack), and once used also has the device with its UDP socket and keepalives.
- VLESS with `reverse` keeps its monitor task: the removed outbound keeps dialing the server every 2 s.
- Same for MASQUE's tunnel. VLESS with `testpre` gets closed too, but its pre-connects only stop reliably with #7113: on main, `Close()` stops just the goroutines waiting to hand over a connection, not the ones redialing an unreachable server.

This shows up wherever outbounds are added and removed at runtime through the API, e.g. by panels.

### Changes

- `RemoveHandler` closes the handler it removed. It does so after releasing the manager lock, so a slow `Close()` (WireGuard) doesn't hold up `Select()`/`GetHandler()` for new connections. Removing an unknown tag still returns nil, and a removed handler is closed only once, since `Manager.Close()` no longer sees it.
- VLESS starts the reverse 2 s after the outbound is created (a goroutine in `New()`), so an outbound removed within those 2 s would still start it after `Close()`. `Reverse.Start()` is now a no-op once `Reverse.Close()` has run.

The other callers of `RemoveHandler` (commander, metrics, reverse portal, VLESS inbound's reverse) remove their own internal outbounds, whose `Close()` is a no-op or idempotent.

Connections already in flight on a removed outbound behave as before unless its `Close()` tears them down (WireGuard, MASQUE). A reverse bridge that is already connected is left to end on its own; only new ones stop.

### Reproduction (on 836a6fe)

Client: `api` with `HandlerService` behind a dokodemo-door inbound, `freedom` as the only configured outbound. Server: a plain TCP listener that only counts accepted connections.

**VLESS `reverse`**: the outbound is added with `xray api ado` and removed with `xray api rmo`. Afterwards `xray api lso` lists only the `freedom` outbound in all runs.

| `rmo` after `ado` | build | accepts at `rmo` | 3 s later | 13 s later |
|---|---|---:|---:|---:|
| 7 s | main | 3 | 4 | 9 |
| 7 s | this PR | 3 | 3 | 3 |
| 0.5 s | main | 0 | 1 | 6 |
| 0.5 s | this PR | 0 | 0 | 0 |

**WireGuard** (`noKernelTun: true`): five outbounds, each added with `ado` and removed right away with `rmo`. Goroutines from the `metrics` listener's `/debug/pprof/goroutine`: main 11 → 72, this PR 11 → 12.

### Tests

- New `TestRemoveHandlerClosesHandler` (on main the handler is closed 0 times) and `TestReverseNotStartedAfterClose` (on main the monitor runs once).
- `go test ./...` except `testing/scenarios`: the only failures also fail on main, tests that need `resources/geo*.dat` or network access.
- `go test ./testing/scenarios`: pass.

```markdown
Follow-up to #6487, covering the startup-padding part of #6732.

Adds an optional `padding` array to XMC settings with configurable direction per turn:

```json

issues.title: Bound shutdown after termination signal
issues.body:
This change prevents Xray from waiting indefinitely during graceful shutdown after receiving SIGTERM or interrupt.

Previously, shutdown depended on the deferred server.Close() call returning. If any feature Close() path blocked, the process could stay alive while listeners or active connections continued operating. This made stale Xray processes difficult to detect, especially when another process could bind the same port.

Now Xray runs server.Close() explicitly after receiving a termination signal and waits up to 10 seconds. If shutdown does not complete in time, the process exits with code 1 so supervisors can treat it as a failed shutdown and avoid leaving a functional stale process behind.

This issue was most visible on mobile clients. Some apps, such as Telegram proxy-style traffic, may continue using an already-established path even when the VPN/client UI appears disabled. If the old Xray process remains alive during a stuck shutdown, those connections can continue transferring traffic and updating usage counters, making the node look stopped from the client side while traffic is still flowing server-side.

issues.title: TLS : tls spoofing
issues.body:
fix #5964

### RawPacket aka TLS Spoofing

So first lets talk about the idea,

when you connect to a xray server, the censors can see your TLS ClientHello, read the SNI, and figure out what you are doing and block :)

The RawPacket aka TLS spoofing fixes that by injecting a fake TLS ClientHello before the real one Hits.


The fake one carries like a decoy domain (ex. baidu.com) and then the real one carries your actual destination (ex. www.example.com).

A sensor that captures the first packet sees baidu.com and think that you are just browsing, and everything is okay with that, but in reality your connection goes through :)


It can be configured in the `finalmask.tcp` okay? and its only for client side.


### How everything works


When Xray dials a TCP connection and the first `Write()` happens (which also triggers the real TLS handshake) , our Raw Packet setup does the following.

1.builds a fake Tls ClientHello with whatever SNI you want or you have option to provide the raw bytes (b64).

2.Then we. wrap it in a raw TCP/ip packet.

3.Then deliberately we corrupt the TCP header using whatever method is selected okay?

4. Then we shoot it out via a raw socket

5. Then immediately let the real `Write()` go through normally


In short : two packets arrive at the server back to back and the fake one gets dropped by the servers TCP stack because of the corruption and then the real handshake proceeds like nothing happened.


### Config Example

```json
{
  "streamSettings": {
    "finalmask": {
      "tcp": [
        {
          "type": "rawpacket",
          "settings": {
            "sni": "baidu.com",
            "payload": "",
            "method": "wrong-sequence",
            "ttl": 3,
            "count": 1
          }
        }
      ]
    }
  }
}
```


### Available Fields

`sni` : The domain to put in the fake ClientHello. If you set this, it will auto generate a valid TLS ClientHello for you automatically. If you set `payload` and `sni` same time , sni wins here.

```
"sni": "baidu.com"
```

`payload` : If you don't want an auto gnrated ClientHello, then just encode your raw bytes that you want into base64 and put them here. I have added an option to do it from command line also. Do like this 

```
 xray tls fake-hello google.com
 ```

It will out the thing and then just copy paste.


Note : If `sni` and payload are empty or not set , the raw packet does nothing and the connection goes through normally.


`method` : It defines how we corrupt the fake packet so the server drops it.

`wrong-sequence` : It duplicates the sequence number (looks like a retransmission so server drops it)

So we grab the kernels `snd_nxt` ( the next sequence number the kernel expects to send), then subtract the length of the fake payload and then use that as the sequence number of the injected packet. The results then is a duplicate of the. last segment, so the receivers TCP stack sees it as a retransmit at best, or like out of window at worst and then drops it.


`wrong-checksum`: It flips all the bits in the TCP checksum (so server sees a bad checksum and drops it)

We build the packet with a correct checksum and then flip every bit(^0xFFFF). The receiver then validates the checksum and its wrong, so the packet goes in trash.

`wrong-ack`: It sets ACK number way outside the receive window (so server sends dup ACK then drops it)

It sets the ACK number to `rcv_nxt - window/2` and that's way outside of the receivers window, and the kernel responds with a dup ACK containing the correct sequence number, then drops it.

`wrong-md5` : This adds a fake TCP MD5 signature option and server without MD5 drops it

Here we append a TCP option with kind=19 and length=18 to the TCP header. The kind 19 is the MD5 signature option (RFC 2385), if the receiver doesn't use TCP MD5 (which is basically everything except some BGP routers), it sees an unknown option

issues.title: sockopt.interface: when the interface does not exist, the dial silently goes unbound (can loop back into TUN)
issues.body:
### Integrity requirements

- [x] I have read all the comments in the issue template and ensured that this issue meet the requirements.
- [x] I confirm that I have read the documentation, understand the meaning of all the configuration items I wrote, and did not pile up seemingly useful options or default values.
- [x] I provided the complete config and logs, rather than just providing the truncated parts based on my own judgment.
- [x] I searched issues and did not find any similar issues.
- [x] The problem can be successfully reproduced in the latest Release

### Description

If an outbound has `streamSettings.sockopt.interface` set and that interface does not exist at dial time, Xray does not fail the dial. It logs `failed to apply socket options > failed to get interface ...` at **Info** level and opens the connection without any binding, so it follows the system routing table.

`transport/internet/system_dialer.go` (v26.10.10, lines 134-139; same in v26.9.9) only logs the error returned by `applyOutboundSocketOptions` and goes on to `dialer.DialContext`. The UDP path does the same (lines 77-81). The error itself comes from `net.InterfaceByName` in `transport/internet/sockopt_darwin.go:136-140`. From reading the source, Linux takes the same path (the error is logged, not returned); I tested macOS only.

Why this matters. A typical full-tunnel setup on a desktop routes everything into a TUN interface handled by Xray (default route split as 0.0.0.0/1 + 128.0.0.0/1 into the TUN), and binds outbounds with `sockopt.interface` so that their own sockets do not enter the TUN again. If the bound interface goes away, the fallback sends the outbound's sockets into the TUN, Xray routes them to the same outbound, and the connection loops.

We hit this loop in practice on macOS. A separate OpenVPN client provided a corporate network through its own utun interface, and the corporate subnet was routed to a freedom outbound so that it would follow that VPN's route. At night the OpenVPN client lost its connection and its utun interface was removed. From then on, every connection to the corporate subnet (including DNS queries to the corporate DNS server) entered the TUN, came back to the same outbound and entered the TUN again. When we looked, there were about 8,000 looped connections, all 16,384 ephemeral ports were in use, and other processes on the host got `EADDRNOTAVAIL` (`Can't assign requested address`) on connect until the loop was broken by restarting Xray.

In that incident the outbound had no `sockopt.interface` at all, so the loop itself is a config problem. The obvious fix is to bind the outbound to the other VPN's interface (`"interface": "utunN"`), so that it can never fall into the TUN. That does not work because of this issue: once the interface disappears, the binding is skipped and the loop is back. The only visible sign is an Info-level log line, which is hidden at the usual `warning` level.

Expected: if the interface named in `sockopt.interface` cannot be found, the dial fails (fail closed), as a bound socket does when its interface has no route. At the very least the error should be logged as a warning. A silent fallback to the routing table defeats the purpose of binding: it can send traffic into a tunnel (loop) or past it (leak).

### Reproduction Method

No server and no TUN are needed. Run Xray with the config below (interface `utun99` does not exist) and send a request through the SOCKS inbound:

```
curl --socks5-hostname 127.0.0.1:1080 http://example.com/
```

Result: HTTP 200. The log shows that the interface was not found and the connection was opened anyway; its local endpoint is the address of whatever interface the routing table chose (on our machine, the address of a TUN interface that held the default route).

For comparison, with `"interface": "en0"` the same request goes out through en0 (local endpoint is en0's address) and no error is logged.

Expected result: the connection through the outbound bound

issues.title: Outbound: Close a removed handler and its connections
issues.body:
RemoveOutbound only drops the handler from the outbound manager and never closes it. A removed WireGuard outbound keeps its device up and keeps sending keepalives to the peer, and connections through any removed outbound keep running. The inbound manager already closes a removed handler.

Now RemoveHandler closes the handler, outside the manager's lock. Close cancels a context that each dispatch is tied to, so freedom, VLESS and the other outbounds end their connections too. Mux client connections are dialed under that context as well; otherwise a session behind an inbound that hands the outbound a pipe (VMess, Trojan, Shadowsocks, HTTP) lives on in the shared mux connection.

Without tests it is 35 added and 7 removed lines in 3 files. The tests remove an outbound through the API while a connection goes through it, for WireGuard (no packet reaches the peer afterwards), freedom and a mux outbound behind a Shadowsocks inbound. Each fails on main.

Independent of #7166. Removing an inbound still leaves its connections running; that is not changed here.

The fourth box is unchecked on purpose: #6124 shows the same symptom for one download. It was closed together with #4878 by #6834, which fixed the close_notify leak but not the switch. Details below.

### Description

Since #5179 (first released in v25.12.1), `VisionWriter` switches to direct copy only when a whole read batch is made of complete TLS application-data records:

https://github.com/XTLS/Xray-core/blob/701af60772cda123492f86e383e1fdba066614a9/proxy/proxy.go#L362-L369

`IsCompleteRecord` ([proxy.go#L408-L460](https://github.com/XTLS/Xray-core/blob/701af60772cda123492f86e383e1fdba066614a9/proxy/proxy.go#L408-L460)) looks at one batch at a time and keeps no state between batches. For TLS 1.3 nothing else ends the padding: the shortcut at [L381](https://github.com/XTLS/Xray-core/blob/701af60772cda123492f86e383e1fdba066614a9/proxy/proxy.go#L381) only applies to traffic that is not TLS 1.2+. Once a batch ends inside a record, the next batch starts inside a record and cannot pass. The switch then only happens if two reads in a row both end exactly on a record boundary.

With a sender that writes full-size records back to back, that doesn't happen:

- The first read after the handshake is a single 8 KiB buffer. `ReadVReader` starts with one `buf.Size` buffer and only adds more after a full read ([readv_reader.go#L63-L70](https://github.com/XTLS/Xray-core/blob/701af60772cda123492f86e383e1fdba066614a9/common/buf/readv_reader.go#L63-L70), [#L124-L145](https://github.com/XTLS/Xray-core/blob/701af60772cda123492f86e383e1fdba066614a9/common/buf/readv_reader.go#L124-L145)). So when the handshake fits in 8 KiB, as it does here, the first 16 KiB record (16,406 bytes on the wire) is always cut. In the upload log below, the first batch is the client's ChangeCipherSpec + Finished (64 bytes) plus the first 8,128 bytes of the first record.
- Later reads take up to 8 × 8 KiB. Whenever data waits in the socket, because the proxy or the link behind it is slower than the sender, every read is a full 64 KiB. Two full reads in a row can never both end on a record boundary, because 65,536 is not a multiple of 16,406. So the check can only pass next to a read that drains the socket, which needs the proxy to catch up with the sender.

The download batches come straight from freedom's reads of the target socket ([freedom.go#L435](https://github.com/XTLS/Xray-core/blob/701af60772cda123492f86e383e1fdba066614a9/proxy/freedom/freedom.go#L435), [proxy.go#L790-L797](https://github.com/XTLS/Xray-core/blob/701af60772cda123492f86e383e1fdba066614a9/proxy/proxy.go#L790-L797)). The upload batches are the client inbound's reads ([outbound.go#L367](https://github.com/XTLS/Xray-core/blob/701af60772cda123492f86e383e1fdba066614a9/proxy/vless/outbound/outbound.go#L367)).

So the connection stays in padding mode for the whole transfer. Each buffer is reshaped and padded, the inner TLS stream is encrypted a second time by the outer TLS, and neither direct copy nor, for downloads, splice ever starts. `CommandPaddingDirect` is only sent after the payload, when a short trailing record arrives alone (here the receiver's 1-byte reply or a close_notify).

Proxy: Close a removed user's connections
issues.body:
RemoveUser only takes the user out of the validator, so a removed user keeps every connection it already has. Panels remove users this way when they run out of traffic or time, and those users keep using traffic (#5844 has one at 18 GB on a 1 GB limit).

#5844 solves it with a connection tracker: each connection is registered in a map and wrapped to count bytes, with a gRPC API on top, about 3400 lines in 34 files. This PR follows RPRX's suggestion there instead: each MemoryUser carries a context that RemoveUser cancels, and each inbound ties its connections to it with context.AfterFunc, which cancels the connection's ctx and closes the conn. Nothing runs per read or write and nothing is registered anywhere. There is no connection API here, only the close.

Without tests it is 131 added and 12 removed lines in 16 files, a few lines per inbound: VLESS (Mux, Vision and reverse), VMess, Trojan, Shadowsocks, SS2022 multi-user, Hysteria and WireGuard. Hysteria closes the whole QUIC connection, since it authenticates only once per connection, and Shadowsocks and SS2022 UDP sessions end too. The UDP worker also no longer removes a newer conn of the same client when an old one is closed from outside.

The tests (678 lines, mostly the scenario harness) remove a user through the API while it has live connections on each inbound. Every case fails on main.

Removing a user and adding it back unchanged now drops its connections once.

issues.title: System dialer: fail the dial when sockopt.interface cannot be applied
issues.body:
Fixes #7160.

## Problem

With `sockopt.interface` set and the interface missing at dial time, Xray logs the bind error at info level and dials anyway, unbound. The connection then follows the routing table — which is exactly what the binding exists to prevent. In the setup from #7160 the fallback loops the connection back into the TUN: about 8,000 looped connections, all 16,384 ephemeral ports in use on the host, `EADDRNOTAVAIL` for other processes, until a restart.

## Change

The two `Control` closures in `system_dialer.go` (tcp dial and udp listen-packet) now propagate the error when `sockopt.Interface` is set, so the dial fails closed — the same way it already fails when the interface has no route. The dial failure is then reported by the usual path (freedom logs `failed to open connection > failed to bind to interface <name> > no such device`), visible at normal log levels instead of the info-only line it was.

Since `RawConn.Control` runs the option application inside a callback that cannot return an error itself, the error is captured and returned from the closure after `Control` completes.

Scope is deliberately limited to the interface option: other sockopt errors (TCP_FASTOPEN, SO_MARK, tcpCongestion) keep the current log-and-continue behavior, because support for those varies across kernels and systems, and configs in the wild rely on the setsockopt being ignored where the kernel refuses it. Unbound dialing is different though — what replaces the missing binding is never acceptable, it loops or leaks.

Also names the interface in the linux (`BindToDevice`) and windows (`InterfaceByName`) error wrappers, the way the darwin one already does, so the failing value shows up in the error:

```
failed to open connection to tcp:... > failed to dial to dest > dial tcp ...: failed to bind to interface nosuchif0 > no such device
```

## Tests

- `TestDialInterfaceMissing` in `dialer_test.go`: tcp and udp dials to a working listener with `sockopt.interface: "nosuchif0"`, both must return an error naming the interface (before the change, both succeeded unbound; the reporter's reproduction is the same thing seen through a socks inbound);
- full test suite of the package passes; also checked by hand with two xray binaries (vless + xhttp, socks inbound, freedom outbound bound to a nonexistent interface): the request now fails with the error above instead of going through.

issues.title: XHTTP: packet-down in stream-down with downlink keep-alive
issues.body:
# XHTTP: packet-down in stream-down with downlink keep-alive

Follows RPRX's packet-down design in https://github.com/XTLS/Xray-core/pull/6755#issuecomment-5720463978, which was written while closing the earlier downlink-resume attempt (#6755). That attempt was rejected because "restore connection" is too complex, with latency, ACK and so on. This one does not attempt connection restoration at all. No reconnection, no state machine, nothing to tune: each stream-down GET stays a single request; if the GET dies, the connection dies the ordinary way.

## Problem (from #4846)

CDNs kill a stream-down GET on body inactivity. This matters during uploads: with packet-up the uplink posts keep flowing, but the downlink proxy payload only arrives while the origin sends, so during a pure upload the GET idles and gets cut. Same story for any target that goes quiet for a while after responding.

## What this PR adds

When enabled on both ends, the stream-down response body is cut into packet-down frames with the five elements from the design comment:

- omittable session id excerpt: first 8 bytes of the session id, present on data and keep-alive frames (absent in stream-one where the session id is empty)
- omittable packet seq: uint64, counting data/keep-alive frames per stream-down GET
- mandatory type: data or padding
- mandatory length: uint16
- payload

Use today is the first one from the design comment: downlink keep-alive. While the downlink has been idle for a whole period, the server writes a padding frame (base62, in the spirit of tokenish x-padding) instead of staying silent. Everything the dispatcher sends rides in data frames, which is what lets the client tell padding apart from payload safely; the seq keeps the format ready for the future uses listed in the design comment (retransmission, multi-path-down) without another wire change.

h1, h2 and h3 are covered, since the framers sit on the body, not on a specific transport. stream-one gets the same treatment on its single response body. Browser dialer is out of scope for now: it has no place to read the response header that confirms the framing.

## Negotiation

Strictly opt-in and per request, so old servers are unaffected and nothing breaks behind middleboxes:

1. client config has packetDown: XHTTP stream requests not used as pure uplink (stream-down GET, stream-one request) carry X-Packet-Down: 1
2. server has packetDown configured and sees the marker: it answers with X-Packet-Down: 1 on the response, and frames; without the confirmed header the client never parses frames
3. any other combination: byte-identical wire format as today

## Config

```jsonc
"xhttpSettings": {
  "path": "/sh",
  "packetDown": {              // absent = disabled, as today
    "keepAlive": true,
    "keepAlivePeriod": "10-30",  // seconds; padded when inactive this long. defaults to 10-30
    "keepAliveLength": "24-64"   // padding size. defaults to 24-64
  }
}
```

Server side is the same block in the inbound; the server only honors the feature when the client asks.

## Not in this PR (deliberately)

- obfs of the frames (later, per the design comment)
- retransmission, multi-path-down, same-packet racing, ACK: the format carries seq and the session excerpt, but none of the machinery, exactly like packet-up carries seq today without using it
- nothing about #4846's larger downlink freeze problem (the 15-20 KB per TCP connection cut): this only discards the CDN idle timer, it does not split data across connections

## Tests

- packet_down_test.go: frame round trip (with/without excerpt, with/without seq), byte-stream shaped like a socket, splitting payloads larger than one frame, padding skipped, malformed frame rejected, keep-alive written when idle, keep-alive suppressed while active, config normalization
- splithttp_test.go: full listen/dial round trip with packet-down on both end (100 KiB), and the fallback case with the client setting present but the server without one
- infra/conf: JSON un

Ai said this:

on the hook bitmask. a shared mask gives every state one answer and costs an atomic load per call, and more to the point it is what lets a mask decide not to wrap a connection at all when its hook is missing, which a live lookup cannot undo after the fact. clearing bits and never setting them makes dynamic registration impossible by construction instead of by convention, which is the property you asked for. a live lookup would always match the state that is about to run and would leave room for re-registration, but four `GetGlobal` lookups are about 4% of one header hook call on a packet, and states would then start behaving differently from one another, which is harder to reason about than one shared answer. the real cost of probing once is a script that defines a hook conditionally, by time or by chance, which can be probed wrong, so the docs should say hooks are defined at the top level, and logging the hooks found at init would make a typo visible instead of silent.

on the declaration style. globals need no core change, they are the shape dns and router already ship, and there is nothing for the engine to inject; the cost is that a mistake is silent, `HandleHeaderWirte` simply means no hook and the mask passes traffic through instead of failing. a returned table is explicit and discoverable, a natural place for metadata later, and it lets a hook be a closure instead of a global, but it needs `PCall(0, 1)` plus per state storage in core, and the engine would then want to inject `unregister`, which dns and router can never honour, so that debt lands on the two that cannot unload. a register call is the only one of the three that allows registration inside a closure or a branch, which is exactly what several state instances cannot support, so ruling it out is right. globals now, with a standalone unload function later if one is ever needed, leaves the least behind.

on permission levels. gating early costs little and spares you reviewing the same risk twice; the counter risk is freezing the wrong split while nothing uses it yet. the surface here is narrow: no filesystem, no new sockets, only the connection the mask was handed, with caps on bytes and packets and a timeout per hook. the one api that can hold a pooled state is `stream:Sleep`, and a blocking api has to respect the state context or the timeout is decoration and a level buys nothing. a split that should survive contact is everything that only produces bytes, the noise plan, the header builder and the packet view, at the lowest level, with raw stream read and write plus sleep one level above, so that `register` simply does not install the stream object below that level and no call site has to change when signing comes back.

bitmask is in. the engine keeps an `atomic.Uint32`, the first state fills it and `validate` rejects a script with no hook at all. a hook a script drops is cleared for the whole engine so every other state short circuits it too, and bits only ever get cleared, never set, so nothing can register one later even by accident. the wrap decision stays where it was: a mask whose hook the script doesn't define returns the raw conn and isn't wrapped at all, the bit only decides whether an already wrapped conn still goes into Lua. two tests for it, one drops `HandleHeaderWrite` after the first packet and the rest go out bare, one drops `HandleNoise` and a new destination gets no noise either.

agreed on keeping the globals, and the injected `unregister` is the right reason. two more in favour: `NewState` runs the chunk with `L.PCall(0, 0, nil)`, so whatever a script returns is dropped today and the table would need a core change first, and `HandleDNSQuery`/`HandleRoute` are already released (#6823 merged at 09:01 on the 10th, v26.10.10 tagged at 09:21 the same day), so globals are the released convention and not only the current one. starting from zero i'd have said the table, since that's what pooled plugin hosts tend to do (kong plugins end with `return Handler`, plain lua modules `return M`), but with those two released and unable to unload, a standalone function later beats a table field they'd never implement.

comments.issue_title: REALITY fails with www.microsoft.com target when Certificate TLS record is 8273 bytes (>8192 hardcoded limit)
comments.body:
I can confirm this issue on **Xray 26.6.27**, managed by **3x-ui 3.6.0**, running on **Ubuntu 24.04**.

VLESS TCP + REALITY + Vision stopped passing traffic when using `www.microsoft.com:443` as the REALITY target. The server accepted connections, but websites would not load through the VPN.

Packet capture showed that port 443 was reachable and the TCP handshake completed. The client then sent approximately 1.9 KB of initial data. The server acknowledged it and closed the connection with FIN, without sending any TLS payload. The client kept retrying.

To isolate the failure, we ran a temporary Xray client on the VPS and connected to the existing inbound over loopback. The same failure occurred locally, so neither the home network nor ISP filtering was required to reproduce it. Ordinary TLS connections from the VPS to Microsoft succeeded.

An isolated test server using the same REALITY credentials produced these diagnostic lines:

```text
hs.c.conn == conn: true
Certificate: 8273
hs.c.isHandshakeComplete.Load(): false
handshake did not complete successfully
```

REALITY authentication passed, but processing the target’s response failed. Microsoft returned a **8273-byte Certificate TLS record**, exceeding the **8192-byte limit** in the REALITY implementation used by this version.

This explains why checking port availability and establishing an ordinary TLS connection to the target did not reveal the problem: the failure occurred inside REALITY’s handshake processing.

Connectivity was restored by changing the server target and updating the client SNI consistently:

```text
Server target:      www.nvidia.com:443
Server serverNames: ["www.nvidia.com"]
Client SNI:         www.nvidia.com
```

UUIDs, keys, short IDs, port 443 and `flow=xtls-rprx-vision` were preserved. After the change, HTTPS requests through the production TCP inbound returned HTTP 200 with both `chrome` and `firefox` fingerprints. Connectivity from the previously affected home network was also restored.

Clients need to refresh their subscriptions or update the SNI in manually imported profiles. NVIDIA worked for this deployment; the suitability of a target should be tested for each server.

These results confirm the existing issue on version 26.6.27, not a regression in a release containing the fix. The core was not upgraded during this investigation.

yeah, better to settle it now than refactor it later.

-- 1. the engine probes the four hooks once when it builds the pool and keeps them in a struct, and `validate` errors if a script defines none. the point of caching isn't the lookup, it's that a mask whose hook isn't defined returns the raw conn and never gets wrapped, so TCP keeps `Splice` and a packet doesn't go through anything. four `GetGlobal` lookups cost about 4% of one header hook call on a packet and the cached read about 0.03%, so checking live is affordable too if you want scripts to unload hooks later. but a conn that was never wrapped can't grow a hook back, so unloading needs the engine rebuilt and a reload already does that. a global script that isn't pooled can just call `defined()` live, it's the same function.

comments.body:
Codex sol 6.1

Regarding packet sizes and QUIC: there are still limits, both in DNS and in this XDNS implementation. Reviewed source: `ca65d74c79b0715e6a1370db896c053df52ea719`.

- DNS over TCP and DoH allow DNS messages up to **65,535 bytes**, but an implementation can impose a smaller limit. EDNS0 advertises UDP receive capacity; it does not remove the TCP/DoH message limits. DoH servers must ignore the EDNS UDP payload-size advertisement. [RFC 1035 §4.2.2](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc1035.html#section-4.2.2), [RFC 8484 §6](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8484.html#section-6).
- This XDNS implementation has a **4096-byte** receive limit. The [TCP resolver discards frames larger than that](https://github.com/XTLS/Xray-core/blob/ca65d74c79b0715e6a1370db896c053df52ea719/transport/internet/finalmask/xdns/resolver_tcp.go#L76).
- Client-to-server, XDNS [splits larger datagrams across DNS queries](https://github.com/XTLS/Xray-core/blob/ca65d74c79b0715e6a1370db896c053df52ea719/transport/internet/finalmask/xdns/client.go#L193) and reassembles them. Domain-name/label limits and Base32 overhead still constrain each query, but they do not alone prevent larger datagrams.
- Server-to-client, one datagram is **not split across multiple responses**. It must fit in the response budget: **512 bytes without EDNS0**, or at most **4096** with suitable EDNS0 settings on both sides, minus DNS framing and encoding overhead. An oversized queued datagram can be dropped. This [response-budget calculation](https://github.com/XTLS/Xray-core/blob/ca65d74c79b0715e6a1370db896c053df52ea719/transport/internet/finalmask/xdns/resp.go#L32) remains an XDNS application limit even when the resolver transport is TCP.
- The built-in [XDNS resolver currently supports TCP and UDP only](https://github.com/XTLS/Xray-core/blob/ca65d74c79b0715e6a1370db896c053df52ea719/transport/internet/finalmask/xdns/resolver.go#L17). Ordinary Xray DNS support for DoH is a separate mechanism.

**QUIC is possible in principle if the complete tunnel preserves the necessary datagram sizes in both directions.** QUIC requires support for UDP payloads of at least 1200 bytes. Small DNS queries are not inherently a problem if the tunnel reconstructs the complete original datagram, but the downstream response limit still matters. Our tests do not establish that QUIC over XDNS works. [RFC 9000 §14](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9000.html#section-14).

**There is also a separate concrete DNS-over-TCP framing bug.** [The send path](https://github.com/XTLS/Xray-core/blob/ca65d74c79b0715e6a1370db896c053df52ea719/transport/internet/finalmask/xdns/resolver_tcp.go#L127) uses:

```go
binary.Write(r.conn, binary.BigEndian, len(p))
```

`len(p)` has type `int`, which `binary.Write` does not support. The error is ignored, so the two-byte length prefix is not written.

I checked this with a real local TCP connection and a 30-byte DNS query whose ID was `0x1234`. The server read **4660** as the frame length instead of **30**: it was reading the DNS ID because the prefix was missing. With this change, the framing test passes with `-race`:

```go
binary.Write(r.conn, binary.BigEndian, uint16(len(p)))
```

An important clarification about my earlier “XDNS over TCP” reproduction: it tested opening the TCP resolver connection and replacing the canceled context, **not DNS-message transfer**. The actual WireGuard traffic tests used ordinary UDP, not the complete WireGuard-over-XDNS path. That earlier connection test could not detect this framing issue.

This XDNS issue was not introduced by PR #7151 and does not change the conclusions about its WireGuard initialization fix.

comments.body:
I'll be working on these next week & the possibility of implementing them:
> 1. Hybrid discovery: GET for the head, LIST for everything else (3–5×, the big one)
> Right now every segment costs ~10 GETs (head hunt + 6 tails polling every 150–200 ms through an ~880 ms write). Polls — calls that return "not yet" — are pure overhead, likely the majority of your Drive traffic under load.
> 
> But a single files.list returns up to 64 segments for 1 request. The fix: keep the cheap GET hunt for the head segment only (that's your latency — ~371 ms, untouched), and discover everything behind/ahead of it with one periodic LIST sweep per second. Under bulk, per-segment cost drops from ~10 GETs to ~2 (one head GET + 1/64th of a LIST).
> 
> Two reasons this works now whereas the old 64-name probe failed: slots carry data in the body, so descriptions are tiny seq headers — a 64-name LIST response is kilobytes, not the 1.4 MB that choked the old path; and the 450 ms index lag doesn't matter for catch-up traffic that's already pipelined, because freshness is still owned by the head GET.
> 
> 2. Batching is a 10× lever you already partly own
> One segment can carry 1 browser message or 50 — same PATCH. A 60-request refresh arriving as a burst should leave as ~3–6 segments, not 60. Your flushIntervalMs: 10 plus the hold-while-growing logic does this, but verify it's engaging: if your logs show segment counts near request counts during bursts, the hold window wants lengthening (code constant today, not config). Rough economics with batching at 10 msgs/segment: ~6 Drive calls per segment ÷ 10 messages ≈ 0.6 calls per browser message → ~25 browser req/s sustained on a 15/s cap. Without batching: ~2.5/s. Same cap, 10× the browsing.
> 
> 3. Bigger segments for bulk (linear, free)
> PATCH cost is size-independent (~880 ms whether 14 KB or 1 MB), so every doubling of segment size halves PATCHes per megabyte. This is why bulk belongs on 1 MB segments — it's not about bandwidth, it's about buying back 4× the request budget. Small writes are unaffected (they flush as partials either way).
> 
> 4. Spend the budget in priority order when throttled (code-level, small)
> When 403s appear, today's response is a flat 2 s global freeze. Smarter: freeze tails and LIST sweeps first, keep head-hunts and writes flowing — i.e., degrade discovery gracefully instead of stopping the world. Saves the interactive experience precisely when the cap binds.

comments.issue_title: hysteria outbound: stream blocked on flow control is never released after the local connection ends
comments.body:
Implemented and verified; opened a pull request: https://github.com/XTLS/Xray-core/pull/7172

Branch `fix/hysteria-reset-stalled-writes` @ c85f66fa (one file + a transport test). `interConn.Close()` now resets the stream's write side (`CancelWrite`) when the request direction still has a write in flight, so the blocked `Write` returns and the peer drops the unread data and releases its share of the connection-level window. Cleanly finished sessions keep the plain close.

Verified end to end on loopback against a real hysteria v2.11.0 server, using your reproduction (4 uploads to a target that stops reading after ~2 MB, aborted with `SO_LINGER 0`):

- before (10879a4a): 11 fresh requests over ~43 s after the abort never succeed;
- after: the first retry that lands after the aborted sessions idle out succeeds (~6 s after the abort with `connIdle` forced to 5 s in the test client).

The transport test `TestTCPStalledWriteClose` fails on main ("stalled write did not return after close") and passes with the change; it also checks that a new stream can send again and that a cleanly finished stream still delivers FIN + all data.

One scope note: the release happens when the aborted session ends (its own idle timeout, or any other teardown of the session) - the local abort itself is not observable once the writer is wedged, so the idle timeout remains the upper bound with stock servers. This composes with the server-side fix in HyNetworks/hysteria#1703 rather than replacing it.

comments.issue_title: hysteria outbound: stream blocked on flow control is never released after the local connection ends
comments.body:
Traced on main (10879a4a) and reproduced the scenario on loopback: 4 uploads to a target that stops reading after ~2 MB, each writing ~18 MB over 4 s, aborted with `SO_LINGER 0`; a 5th request over the same client connection gets no data within 30 s - same result as your run.

The code confirms it: `interConn.Close()` is `CancelRead(0)` + `stream.Close()`, and nothing ever touches the stream's write side. A `Write` blocked on the flow-control window is only released by `CancelWrite` ("Write will unblock immediately") or the connection closing - `Close()` alone does not wake it, and the FIN it queues cannot be delivered while data is stuck behind the window, so the peer is never told to drop the stream's buffered data. That is why nothing recovers until the session and connection are gone.

Plan: in `interConn.Close()`, when the request side still has a write in flight, cancel the stream's write side (`CancelWrite`, i.e. RESET_STREAM) instead of only queueing the FIN, so the blocked `Write` returns and the RESET reaches the peer, releasing the stream's unread data and crediting the connection-level window. Cleanly finished sessions keep the plain close. Note the teardown itself is still driven by the client's idle timeout when the local abort arrives while the writer is wedged (at that point the abort is not observable), but the release then actually happens instead of never, and it should compose with the server-side fix in HyNetworks/hysteria#1703.

I will add a transport test for the blocked-write case and rerun this rig with the fix, then post the branch here.

comments.issue_title: sockopt.interface: when the interface does not exist, the dial silently goes unbound (can loop back into TUN)
comments.body:
In my case the interface is not down, it is gone. When the OpenVPN client disconnects (here it lost its server and then failed to re-authenticate), macOS destroys its utun interface (`if_detached` in the system log). From then on `net.InterfaceByName("utunN")` fails with `no such network interface` (`transport/internet/sockopt_darwin.go:136-140`), and `system_dialer.go` only logs that at Info and dials without the binding (lines 134-139 for TCP, 77-81 for UDP).

As long as the interface exists, even if it is down, `InterfaceByName` succeeds and `IP_BOUND_IF` is set, so the socket stays bound. The fallback happens only when the interface has disappeared. That is typical for tunnel interfaces (utun/tun/wg/ppp), which are removed when the VPN disconnects and may come back under another name, and for USB or Thunderbolt Ethernet that gets unplugged.

So the fix that would have helped me is to fail the dial when the configured interface cannot be found, instead of dialing unbound.

function HandleDNSQuery(domain, ipv4, ipv6, fake)

Codex astra 6

**I would not accept the complete change yet.** Reviewed head `896acd78b17c8094bc94c0e4f70c3ab4142b136e`. The author added `SetCtx` and [requested a review](https://github.com/XTLS/Xray-core/pull/7151#issuecomment-6190866652).

`SetCtx` works: recovery after a canceled request passes, and repeated `Up` failures do not create new devices. All **6 existing package tests pass with `-race`**.

However, there are three regressions:

1. **Xray panics during startup when DNS Lua is configured.**  
   [`NewClient` now calls `IpcSet`](https://github.com/XTLS/Xray-core/blob/896acd78b17c8094bc94c0e4f70c3ab4142b136e/proxy/wireguard/client.go#L191), which resolves the peer endpoint before `Start`. The Lua pool has not been initialized yet, so the lookup reaches [`Pool.Acquire` with a nil receiver](https://github.com/XTLS/Xray-core/blob/896acd78b17c8094bc94c0e4f70c3ab4142b136e/common/lua/pool.go#L51) and panics. The pool is initialized by [`scriptEngine.start`](https://github.com/XTLS/Xray-core/blob/896acd78b17c8094bc94c0e4f70c3ab4142b136e/app/dns/script.go#L30). Reproduced through ordinary `core.New`; the original version passes.

2. **Startup now depends on outbound order.**  
   If WireGuard appears before the `direct` outbound used by DNS routing, its constructor tries to use `direct` before that handler has been registered. Core [constructs each outbound before registering it and processes them sequentially](https://github.com/XTLS/Xray-core/blob/896acd78b17c8094bc94c0e4f70c3ab4142b136e/core/xray.go#L126). The log reports `non existing outTag: direct`, followed by a startup error. Moving `direct` before WireGuard makes it work. Both orders work on the original version. Tested with a real local DNS server.

3. **The TUN filter breaks recovery after `Down → Up`.**  
   `Down` is forwarded and closes the bind, but the following `Up` is [unconditionally discarded](https://github.com/XTLS/Xray-core/blob/896acd78b17c8094bc94c0e4f70c3ab4142b136e/proxy/wireguard/client.go#L499). Without the filter, the device recovers; with it, it stays down until another request calls `up`. Tested with a real WireGuard device and a replay of the separate events emitted by Linux. This was not an actual kernel-TUN test.

**Suggested changes:**

- Keep `SetCtx` and single-device ownership.
- Resolve the endpoint and apply `IpcSet` on the first runtime attempt, once the dependencies are ready. Preserve retry capability after failure.
- Limit `EventUp` suppression to initialization, preserving subsequent recovery events.
- Add these regression cases to the PR’s tests.

comments.body:
I reproduced the original leak: five failed endpoint lookups increased the goroutine count from 60 to 270. Keeping one device fixes that.

There is still a retry issue: `listenFunc` captures the first call's `ctx`. If that attempt fails and its caller is canceled, the next attempt still uses the canceled context.

Reproduced with XDNS over TCP: the resolver becomes available, but a fresh request still gets `operation was canceled`.

For the current head `7a7f899a`, keep the device and refresh `listenFunc` before retrying.

In `proxy/wireguard/client.go`, remove the early block from `Handler.up`:

```go
if h.dev != nil {
	return h.dev.Up()
}
```

After the `listenFunc` definition, before constructing a new `bind`, add:

```go
if h.dev != nil {
	h.dev.Bind().(*bind).setListenFunc(listenFunc)
	return h.dev.Up()
}
```

In `proxy/wireguard/bind.go`, add:

```go
func (b *bind) setListenFunc(f func() (net.PacketConn, error)) {
	b.mu.Lock()
	defer b.mu.Unlock()
	b.listenFunc = f
}
```

`Open` uses the same mutex, so replacing the callback is synchronized with bind opening.

The reproduction and fix were tested on `82281867`: without the callback refresh, the recovery test fails; with it, the whole WireGuard package passes with `-race` on Windows, including the original PR test. The snippets above are adjusted to the current `up` layout; I have not rerun the tests on `7a7f899a`.

issues.body:
**Describe the bug**

  On Linux, client 5.0.1.5 fails to read the routing table and never installs
  exclusion routes for the VPN endpoint. With `0.0.0.0/1` and `128.0.0.0/1`
  pointing at the tunnel, WireGuard packets addressed to the server are routed
  back into the tunnel itself, creating a routing loop. Packets grow with each
  iteration until the socket rejects them with `sendmmsg: message too long`.

  Client 4.8.21 on the very same machine installs the routes correctly and works.
  The issue is protocol-independent — reproduced with both AmneziaWG 2.0 and 3.1
  servers.

  **To Reproduce**

  Steps to reproduce the behavior:
  1. Install 5.0.1.5 on Ubuntu 24.04 with a normal DHCP default route
  2. Connect to any AmneziaWG server
  3. Run `ip route get <server-ip>` — it points at the tunnel (`dev amn0`) instead
     of the physical gateway
  4. See `sendmmsg: message too long` in the daemon log; no traffic passes

  **Expected behavior**

  The daemon should add an exclusion route for the server endpoint through the
  physical default gateway, as 4.8.21 does:
  ```
  <server-ip> via 192.168.31.1 dev wlp0s20f3
  ```

  **Log files**

  Same 15-second window, two client versions on one machine:

  | Log line | 5.0.1.5 | 4.8.21 |
  |---|---|---|
  | `Error in received packet: Numerical argument out of domain` | 10 | 0 |
  | `No default gateway available, skipping exclusion route` | 10 | 0 |
  | exclusion routes actually installed | none | all |

5.0.1.5:
  ```
  LinuxRouteMonitor : Adding exclusion route for <server-ip>/32
  Error in received packet: No such file or directory
  LinuxRouteMonitor : No default gateway available, skipping exclusion route
  ...
  WireguardGo : ERROR: (amn0) peer(XXXX…) - Failed to send data packets:
                write udp 0.0.0.0:54793: sendmmsg: message too long
  ```
  
  4.8.21, same step:
  ```
  LinuxRouteMonitor : Adding exclusion route for <server-ip>/32
  ```
  (no warning, route present in `ip route`)
  
  Other errors present in both versions, possibly related:
  ``` 
  Error: argument "amnvpnrt" is wrong: table id value is invalid
  mkdir: cannot create directory '/sys/fs/cgroup/net_cls/amnvpnexclusions/'
  LinuxRouteMonitor : Adding exclusion route for /999999 → Invalid destination prefix
  net_cls cgroup v1 not available, traffic splitting disabled
  ```
  
  **Screenshots**
  
  N/A — the client reports "Connected".

  **Desktop (please complete the following information):**
   - OS: Ubuntu 24.04.4 LTS (kernel 6.17), KDE Plasma / X11
   - Version: 5.0.1.5 (regression — 4.8.21 works)

  **Smartphone (please complete the following information):**
   - Not affected — mobile clients handle routing through the OS VPN API

  **Server (please complete the following information):**
   - OS: Ubuntu 24.04, Docker

**Additional context**
  
  Workaround — add the exclusion route manually before connecting:
  ```
  sudo ip route add <server-ip> via <lan-gateway> dev <iface>
  ```
  The loop disappears and `sendmmsg: message too long` stops.
  
  Possibly related: #1498, #1357, #2048 — all report "connected but no internet"
  on Linux with the same `amnvpnrt` / `Invalid destination prefix` log noise.

issues.title: [Windows 11 26H2] Built-in AmneziaWG fails with WSAEFAULT, while standalone AmneziaWG 3.1.0 works
issues.body:
**Describe the bug**

The AmneziaWG connection built into AmneziaVPN 5.0.3.0 fails on Windows 11 26H2.

The tunnel interface is created successfully, but the client cannot send or receive UDP packets. The service log repeatedly reports errors from `WSASendMsg` and `WSARecvMsg`:

```text
wsasendmsg: The system detected an invalid pointer address in attempting to use a pointer argument in a call.

wsarecvmsg: The system detected an invalid pointer address in attempting to use a pointer argument in a call.
```

As a result, the AmneziaWG handshake never completes.

## Environment

- AmneziaVPN: 5.0.3.0
- Windows: Windows 11 26H2
- Windows build: 26300
- Architecture: x64
- Wintun: 0.14
- Protocol: AmneziaWG
- Standalone AmneziaWG for Windows: 3.1.0

## Troubleshooting performed

I tried the following without success:

- Rebooted the laptop
- Disabled split tunneling
- Disabled Kill Switch
- Confirmed that ByeDPI and Zapret are not installed
- Confirmed that DNS settings are obtained automatically through DHCP
- Flushed and renewed the network configuration
- Checked the Winsock catalog
- Checked installed network filters
- Confirmed that AdGuard and other third-party Winsock providers are not installed

The same AmneziaWG configuration works correctly:

- On a mobile phone connected to the same Wi-Fi network
- In standalone AmneziaWG for Windows 3.1.0 on the same laptop

This confirms that the server, configuration, Wi-Fi connection, UDP connectivity, and MTU are working correctly.

## Additional observations

AmneziaVPN automatically sets the tunnel MTU to 1376. The failure occurs before the first UDP handshake packet can be sent, so changing the MTU or DNS settings does not appear relevant.

Standalone AmneziaWG 3.1.0 works correctly with exactly the same configuration on the same Windows installation.

This strongly suggests a regression or incompatibility in the AmneziaWG tunnel implementation bundled with AmneziaVPN 5.0.3.0 on Windows 11 26H2.

## Workaround

I currently use standalone AmneziaWG for Windows for AWG connections. AmneziaVPN can still be used for VLESS.

Logs attached.

[AmneziaVPN.essentials.log](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/33356106/AmneziaVPN.essentials.log)

issues.title: [macOS][VLESS] Split tunnel exclusion for connected LAN subnet routes via router and breaks LAN access
issues.body:
## Summary

On macOS, AmneziaVPN site-based split tunneling in “Addresses from the list should not be accessed via VPN” mode breaks access to a directly connected LAN subnet when that subnet is added to the exclusion list. The client installs the subnet route via the LAN router instead of on-link via Wi-Fi.

## Environment

- macOS 27.0 (26A428), Wi-Fi `en0`
- AmneziaVPN 5.0.3.0 and 5.0.2.1 macOS `.pkg` builds (both reproduced)
- Amnezia Premium, VLESS/XRay connection
- LAN: `192.168.31.0/24`; Mac: `192.168.31.105`; router: `192.168.31.1`
- Site-based split tunneling enabled, “Addresses from the list should not be accessed via VPN”, with `192.168.31.0/24` in the list

## Reproduction

1. Connect Wi-Fi on `192.168.31.0/24` and confirm a LAN host such as `192.168.31.47` is reachable directly.
2. Add `192.168.31.0/24` to site-based split tunneling exclusions and connect VLESS.
3. Run `netstat -rn -f inet`, `route -n get 192.168.31.47`, and `ping 192.168.31.47`.

## Actual

The client creates this route:

```text
192.168.31/24  192.168.31.1  UGSc  en0
```

The LAN host does not answer. An Ethernet capture on `en0` shows ICMP packets for `192.168.31.47` sent to the router's MAC address, not the LAN host's MAC. The router can return `Destination Port Unreachable`.

Removing `192.168.31.0/24` from the exclusion list removes the bad gateway route, but traffic for the LAN subnet then follows the VPN `/1` route and the host remains unreachable. A temporary direct on-link route for the subnet through `en0` immediately restores ping and ARP resolution of the LAN host. All temporary routes were removed after diagnosis.

## Expected

The connected `192.168.31.0/24` subnet should remain reachable on-link through `en0` while the VPN is connected. If explicitly excluded, the client should not route same-subnet packets through `192.168.31.1`.

## Related reports

- #2830 reports a different Windows route-capture problem affecting connected LAN subnets.
- #2937 / #2973 concern loss of CIDR prefix during input normalization; the full `/24` is present in the route here, so this is separate.
